We were surprised by the color variation in this species and pleased to see the distinctive reddish tergal segments 4-5 of this individual.; The specific plants it was foraging on were in early bloom and were producing copious nectar, because of the duration of foraging on each flower.  Other nearly plants are just forming floral whorls, while others have not differentiated flowers on growing tips yet.  It will be a long bloom period for the black sage this year, which  means extended food availability for foragers, provided high temperatures do not cut it short.

I found this adorable bee exhausted in my yard at sunset and she could no longer fly. We are having a drought here. I did not want her to get eaten by or to sting my dogs or to be eaten by one of the many widows that come out to hunt at night in my yard so I put her a jar with air holes and two paper towels. I dipped the corner of one in water. After spending time with the water she snuggled into the middle of the towels and rested. She slept all crashed out on her side like the others I used this process on. They really look like they might be dead but really are just sleeping. I opened her jar and pulled out the towels and she was still resting but about half an hour in dappled sunlight did the trick and she flew away. Yay!

On Canyon View Loop Trail. B. crotchii is Endemic in California. Conservation Status: Endangered (EN) (IUCN Red List). BB foraging on ? yellow blossoms. Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=bombus+crotchii xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

Two Crotch's Bumble Bees (Bombus crotchii) were observed on Black Sage (Salvia mellifera) at the Claremont Colleges Bernard Field Station (BFS). These bees were conspicuously large, so I think they were queens, which would be consistent with the March sighting date. The Black Sage plants these bees were on are part of the plantings around the Robert Redford Conservancy for Southern California Sustainability. The plantings are all of native plants that occur on the BFS, and they were propagated by California Botanic Garden from indigenous plants on the site. This individual had something on the back of its thorax that I think are pollinia. I am not sure what the source of these might be. Nothing blooming at the BFS at the time had pollinia. It's possible some of the neighboring houses had orchids in bloom. At least one of the neighbors has grown orchids in the past. The observation for the other individual seen at the same time is here - https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/56541203.

Bombus melanopygus is known to be common throughout its range, which includes most of California, the southwestern U.S. deserts, and the Rocky Mountains. There are also records of this species scattered throughout the tundra/taiga regions of Alaska and northern Canada (Williams et al. 2014). Two color forms exist: the dark form (formerly B. edwardsii; Owen et al. 2010) is found primarily in California and Oregon, while the red form (B. melanopygus s. str.) is found in the northern and eastern portions of its range (Koch et al. 2012).

Patches of native shrubs and forbs are dotted throughout the area, including Malosma laurina, Acmispon glaber, Asclepias fascicularis, and Asclepias eriocarpa. Other non-native weeds, including Hirschfeldia incana and Salsola sp. occur along the trail edge. Underside of abdomen appears to be black. Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) Approx length, 16mm. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

Therefore I am leaving this one identified to genus only.

A Yellow-faced Bumblebee (Bombus vosnesenskii) pollinating the flowers of some Coast Woolly Sunflower (Eriophyllum staechadifolium) at Greyhound Rock County Park. The off-white/pale yellow coloration of the hairs on its clypeus (face), anterior scutum (front part of its thorax), and fourth tergites (abdominal segment) is due to natural variation; normally, these hairs are brighter yellow in color. This was a fairly common species at this location. This set has three shots of the same individual bee, taken as it flitted from flower to flower, hunting for nectar. The second shot is probably the best shot of it, as it shows the faint off-white/pale yellow hairs that cover the bee's anterior scutum, head, and clypeus. It also shows that the rest of the bee's hairs are black, except for those on its 4th tergites, which are also the same of-white/pale yellow color. This distribution of yellow and black hairs is a distinctive field mark for this species, separating it from all of the other bumblebees of western North America.

BB foraging on Mustard blossoms. Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. The yellow pollen basket or corbicula is part of the tibia on the hind legs. Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. Black-tailed Bumble Bee (Bombus melanopygus) https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=bombus+melanopygus BugGuide: https://www.bugguide.net/node/view/306658 xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Bumble Bees (Bombus genus) observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=52775&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1 Bumble Bees in the genus Bombus are robust, hairy bees known for their powerful flight and critical role in pollination. Here are Bombus (genus) key traits: • Body structure: They have a large, rounded body divided into head, thorax, and abdomen, typically 1.5–2.5 cm long. Their dense hair (setae) helps trap pollen. • Coloration: Most species show black with yellow, orange, or white banding. Mimicry among species can make visual ID tricky. • Social behavior: They form seasonal colonies led by a single queen. Colonies are smaller than honey bee hives, often under 200 individuals. • Pollination tools: Workers have corbiculae (pollen baskets) on their hind legs and are capable of buzz pollination—vibrating flowers to release pollen, especially useful for crops like tomatoes. • Flight and foraging: They’re strong fliers, active in cooler, cloudier conditions than many other bees. Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. INat susanna_h Hymenoptera (ants, bees, wasps, sawflies) are characterized by two pairs of membranous wings joined by tiny hooks (hamuli), chewing or chewing-sucking mouthparts, complete metamorphosis, and mandibulate mouthparts. Hymenoptera are predators. Hymenoptera order is split into sawflies (broad waist) and wasps/bees/ants (narrow waist). Key Characteristics of Hymenoptera: • Diversity: Over 150,000 described species worldwide, including ants, bees, wasps, and sawflies. • Wings: Typically two pairs of membranous wings; forewings larger than hindwings. The wings are coupled by hamuli (small hooks). Some castes (e.g., worker ants) are wingless. • Body Form:• In Symphyta (sawflies, horntails): broad connection between thorax and abdomen. • In Apocrita (ants, bees, wasps): narrow “wasp waist” between thorax and abdomen. • Mouthparts: Primarily mandibulate (chewing); in bees, modified into a chewing-lapping apparatus for nectar. • Metamorphosis: Holometabolous (complete metamorphosis: egg → larva → pupa → adult). • Feeding:• Sawfly larvae are herbivorous. • Many wasps are predatory or parasitoid, laying eggs in or on other insects. • Bees are nectar and pollen feeders, crucial pollinators. • Ants are omnivorous, with diverse diets. • Sociality: Includes some of the most advanced eusocial insects (ants, honeybees, some wasps), with division of labor, cooperative brood care, and overlapping generations. Most species, however, are solitary. • Ecological Role:• Pollinators (bees, some wasps). • Biological control agents (parasitoid wasps regulating pest populations). • Soil engineers and ecosystem influencers (ants). This bumble bee was very busy on a small patch of Deerweed (Acmispon glaber) beside Johnson's Pasture Road in the Claremont Hills Wilderness Park. It was in the afternoon and windy, and the bee was deep inside the Deerweed and difficult to photograph. It does have a yellow face. I initially thought the yellow abdominal band is on T3, which would indicate Van Dyke's Bumble Bee (Bombus vandykei), and the computer vision agreed. But judging from the comments from experts, it must actually be on T4, which would it's the Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii), which is the most common bumble bee in these parts. This bee was joined by a second individual. I think the photos are all of the same individual, but I'm not 100% certain. The general habitat is dominated by non-native invasive grasses, especially Avena and Bromus species, since this area was historically a pasture. There are, however, patches of native sage scrub and chaparral shrubs, and also native annuals and perennials scattered about.

Link to Coyote Mint (Monardella villosa) host plant observation https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/119579575 Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) Approx length, 16mm. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

Mount Diablo State Park Hiked Mitchell Canyon Road and came back via Eagle Peak Trail. This 7.7 mile loop kicked my butt, especially since I went very slow iNatting like a maniac on the way south before realizing how slow I was going... will I ever learn? I decided to complete the loop rather than turning around so I limited my stops on Eagle Peak Trail, which, in any case, was very steep and slippery in some sections and required attention that wouldn't have allowed for noticing as many species. I didn't have trekking poles and was carrying lots of gear so it was rough! Got here by riding BART from Berryessa to 19th ST Oakland before transferring to Yellow line to Concord, then took the 10 bus to Clayton and bicycled to the park entrance. About 2 hours ride each way but no gas emission and only a little slower than a drive here either way! Yellow-faced Bumble Bees are large – ½ to ¾ inch (1.5 to 2 cm.) long - and their bodies and wings are mostly black. They have a fuzzy yellow head, including a yellow ‘head pile’ on the thorax just behind the actual head (see above) and a single yellow stripe on lower abdomen (males have a partial second stripe). Bombus vosnesenskii lives from about San Diego throughout most of California(except the desert areas), a little into Nevada around Reno, through Oregon, Washington up into Osoyoos British Columbia. This bumblebee is largely as summer bee with most of the hive living from April to September and is the most common bumblebee of California.

The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx NOT Indiscriminate Cuckoo Bumble Bee (Bombus insularis) Native bee in the Cuckoo Bumble Bees (Psithyrus) Subgenus . BugGuide: https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+insularis "The female of the species is 1.6 to 1.9 centimeters long and just under a centimeter wide. The head is black with tufts of yellow hairs and the thorax is coated in long pale yellow hairs. The legs are hairy black. The abdomen has is black with yellow along the sides. The male is smaller, about half a centimeter wide at the abdomen. The head has long black hairs with small patches of yellow and the abdomen has strips of yellow and black hairs. As in other cuckoo bees, the queen of this species enters the nest of a host species, kills the resident queen, and lives and breeds in the nest tended by the host workers. Host species of this bee include the white-shouldered bumblebee (B. appositus), yellow bumblebee (B. fervidus), yellow-fronted bumblebee (B. flavifrons), Nevada bumblebee (B. nevadensis), and orange-belted bumblebee (B. ternarius). This bee is still common and widespread, though it has declined in some areas and disappeared from a few parts of its historical range. Some of its host species have faced more significant declines. Potential threats include habitat loss, pesticides, pathogens from domesticated pollinators, competition from introduced bees, and climate change." https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/143036-Bombus-insularis

I found this bee situated on the top of a cluster of flowers protruding from a flowerbed. It was most likely in this area because the flowers provide bees with pollen and nectar. Collecting these components are vital in order for this insect to feed and thrive. This is because nectar provides energy and pollen provides essential nutrients, such as proteins. I caught this organism with a net and put it in a jar to observe. This organism was large and fuzzy with numerous branched hairs that covered its body. It was also striped with the colors black and yellow. The first segment of the hind tarsi on the insect was enlarged and bore a pollen basket. While I was observing, the insect flew frantically around the inside the jar the entire time. It emitted a distinctly loud buzzing noise. I found a couple of these organisms across the top of the flower clusters. The insect above was collected and pinned in a safe manner.

They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Bumble Bees (Bombus genus) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=52775&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Irene's Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=630955&user_id=aparrot1 Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) "Bees forage on nectar and pollen--nectar as an energy source and pollen for protein and other nutrients. Included in this family are the European honeybees, Bumble Bees and Carpenter Bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) Approx length, 16mm. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. I spotted this Yellow-faced Bumblebee (Bombus vosensenskii) working a large patch of Rose Clover (Trifolium hirtum) at Russian Ridge Open Space Preserve, and I found myself following it and attempting to take its picture. The shots that came out reasonably well remind me of "Where's Waldo" pictures, with the bee playing the part of Waldo. The best of these shots is the lead photo. Here, the Yellow-faced Bumblebee came close enough for me to take a reasonably decent close-up photo of it, one that fortuitously shows the diagnostic yellow patch on its face. The California Bumblebee (Bombus californicus) is very similar in size and appearance, but lacks this yellow facial patch. The lead photo also shows the yellow band on its thorax, its eyes (one on either side of the yellow face patch), its antenna (emerging from the yellow face patch), and - if you look carefully - a bit of its tongue, which it is inserting into the corolla tube of an individual clover flower for a sip of nectar. Also visible are its two front legs. In the remaining two shots,the bee is partly to mostly obscured by the clover. In Shot 2, you can see the side of the bee's head, which again shows part of the yellow facial patch extending over the crown and just touching the yellow band on its thorax. In Shot 3, the bee is facing away from the camera, so you can easily see its abdomen and semi-translucent wings. Photographed near the main (Alpine Road) trailhead to the Rodge Trail at Russian Ridge Open Space Preserve in San Mateo County, CA.

The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

I observed this Crotch's Bumble Bee feeding on White Sage (Salvia apiana) flowers. "Bombus crotchii inhabits open grassland and scrub habitats. Nesting occurs underground. Males perch and chase moving objects in search of mates. This species is classified as a short-tongued species, whose food plants include Asclepias, Chaenactis, Lupinus, Medicago, Phacelia, and Salvia (Williams et al. 2014). Bumble bees are social insects that live in colonies composed of a queen, workers, and reproductives (males and new queens). Colonies are annual and only the new, mated queens overwinter. These queens emerge from hibernation in the early spring and immediately start foraging for pollen and nectar and begin to search for a nest site. Nests are often located underground in abandoned rodent nests, or above ground in tufts of grass, old bird nests, rock piles, or cavities in dead trees. Initially, the queen does all of the foraging and care for the colony until the first workers emerge and assist with these duties. Bumble bees collect both nectar and pollen of the plants that they pollinate. In general, bumble bees forage from a diversity of plants, although individual species can vary greatly in their plant preferences, largely due to differences in tongue length. Bumble bees are well-known to engage in buzz pollination, a very effective foraging technique in which they sonicate the flowers to vibrate the pollen loose from the anthers. Tomatoes (Solanaceae), blueberries (Ericaceae), and many other important food plants are pollinated by bumble bees in this way."(Endangered Species Coalition)

The simplest difference is that males do not have a stinger, so they cannot sting. Their hind legs are also a good clue: males have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket, while females (workers and queens) have a smooth, shiny area on the hind leg used for carrying pollen. One caution is that female cuckoo bumble bees also lack pollen baskets, so leg hair alone is not always enough. Males usually have more facial hair than females, and in some species this hair is bright yellow and easy to see. Their overall hair tends to be longer and messier, giving them a slightly unkempt look compared with the neater appearance of workers and queens. Behavior also helps. Because males do not collect pollen for a nest, they often sit on flowers for long periods or rest between short flights. They may patrol along hedges, forest edges, or trails while searching for females, flying a repeated route and landing briefly before taking off again. Females behave differently: they move quickly from flower to flower, gather pollen, and rarely spend time resting on blossoms. Seasonal timing is another clue. Females are present throughout the colony’s life cycle, but males become common mainly in late summer and fall, when new queens are emerging and mating takes place. Yellow stripe on top of abdomen does not appear to continue around the underside. Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) Approx length, 16mm. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

Other nearly plants are just forming floral whorls, while others have not differentiated flowers on growing tips yet. It will be a long bloom period for the black sage this year, which means extended food availability for foragers, provided high temperatures do not cut it short.

I found this adorable bee exhausted in my yard at sunset and she could no longer fly. We are having a drought here. I did not want her to get eaten by or to sting my dogs or to be eaten by one of the many widows that come out to hunt at night in my yard so I put her a jar with air holes and two paper towels. I dipped the corner of one in water. After spending time with the water she snuggled into the middle of the towels and rested. She slept all crashed out on her side like the others I used this process on. They really look like they might be dead but really are just sleeping. I opened her jar and pulled out the towels and she was still resting but about half an hour in dappled sunlight did the trick and she flew away. Yay!

Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=bombus+crotchii xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

Bumblebee foraging on Pacific Pea (Lathyrus vestitus) flower. Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) Approx length, 16mm. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

Two Crotch's Bumble Bees (Bombus crotchii) were observed on Black Sage (Salvia mellifera) at the Claremont Colleges Bernard Field Station (BFS). These bees were conspicuously large, so I think they were queens, which would be consistent with the March sighting date. The Black Sage plants these bees were on are part of the plantings around the Robert Redford Conservancy for Southern California Sustainability. The plantings are all of native plants that occur on the BFS, and they were propagated by California Botanic Garden from indigenous plants on the site. This individual had something on the back of its thorax that I think are pollinia. I am not sure what the source of these might be. Nothing blooming at the BFS at the time had pollinia. It's possible some of the neighboring houses had orchids in bloom. At least one of the neighbors has grown orchids in the past. The observation for the other individual seen at the same time is here - https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/56541203.

Bombus melanopygus is known to be common throughout its range, which includes most of California, the southwestern U.S. deserts, and the Rocky Mountains. There are also records of this species scattered throughout the tundra/taiga regions of Alaska and northern Canada (Williams et al. 2014). Two color forms exist: the dark form (formerly B. edwardsii; Owen et al. 2010) is found primarily in California and Oregon, while the red form (B. melanopygus s. str.) is found in the northern and eastern portions of its range (Koch et al. 2012).

Underside of abdomen appears to be black. Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) Approx length, 16mm. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

A Yellow-faced Bumblebee (Bombus vosnesenskii) pollinating the flowers of some Coast Woolly Sunflower (Eriophyllum staechadifolium) at Greyhound Rock County Park. The off-white/pale yellow coloration of the hairs on its clypeus (face), anterior scutum (front part of its thorax), and fourth tergites (abdominal segment) is due to natural variation; normally, these hairs are brighter yellow in color. This was a fairly common species at this location. This set has three shots of the same individual bee, taken as it flitted from flower to flower, hunting for nectar. The second shot is probably the best shot of it, as it shows the faint off-white/pale yellow hairs that cover the bee's anterior scutum, head, and clypeus. It also shows that the rest of the bee's hairs are black, except for those on its 4th tergites, which are also the same of-white/pale yellow color. This distribution of yellow and black hairs is a distinctive field mark for this species, separating it from all of the other bumblebees of western North America.

Here are Bombus (genus) key traits: • Body structure: They have a large, rounded body divided into head, thorax, and abdomen, typically 1.5–2.5 cm long. Their dense hair (setae) helps trap pollen. • Coloration: Most species show black with yellow, orange, or white banding. Mimicry among species can make visual ID tricky. • Social behavior: They form seasonal colonies led by a single queen. Colonies are smaller than honey bee hives, often under 200 individuals. • Pollination tools: Workers have corbiculae (pollen baskets) on their hind legs and are capable of buzz pollination—vibrating flowers to release pollen, especially useful for crops like tomatoes. • Flight and foraging: They’re strong fliers, active in cooler, cloudier conditions than many other bees. Many species are generalist foragers, while some specialize in deep flowers thanks to long tongues. • Defense: Females can sting repeatedly but are generally non-aggressive unless provoked. How to identify if it’s a MALE or FEMALE Bumble Bee: by INat makarii_loskutov who handles many: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Apine Bees (Apinae) Subfamily observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=199939&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=630955&user_id=aparrot1 Photography Tip for Bee and Wasp Identification: "Look at shape first, proportions, abdomen, eyes, antennae length, and wing venation when possible. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Yellow-faced Bumble Bees are large – ½ to ¾ inch (1.5 to 2 cm.) long - and their bodies and wings are mostly black. They have a fuzzy yellow head, including a yellow ‘head pile’ on the thorax just behind the actual head (see above) and a single yellow stripe on lower abdomen (males have a partial second stripe). Bombus vosnesenskii lives from about San Diego throughout most of California(except the desert areas), a little into Nevada around Reno, through Oregon, Washington up into Osoyoos British Columbia. This bumblebee is largely as summer bee with most of the hive living from April to September and is the most common bumblebee of California.

Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx NOT Indiscriminate Cuckoo Bumble Bee (Bombus insularis) Native bee in the Cuckoo Bumble Bees (Psithyrus) Subgenus . The head is black with tufts of yellow hairs and the thorax is coated in long pale yellow hairs. The legs are hairy black. The abdomen has is black with yellow along the sides. The male is smaller, about half a centimeter wide at the abdomen. The head has long black hairs with small patches of yellow and the abdomen has strips of yellow and black hairs. As in other cuckoo bees, the queen of this species enters the nest of a host species, kills the resident queen, and lives and breeds in the nest tended by the host workers. Host species of this bee include the white-shouldered bumblebee (B. appositus), yellow bumblebee (B. fervidus), yellow-fronted bumblebee (B. flavifrons), Nevada bumblebee (B. nevadensis), and orange-belted bumblebee (B. ternarius). This bee is still common and widespread, though it has declined in some areas and disappeared from a few parts of its historical range. Some of its host species have faced more significant declines. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Bumble Bees (Bombus genus) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=52775&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Irene's Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=630955&user_id=aparrot1 Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) "Bees forage on nectar and pollen--nectar as an energy source and pollen for protein and other nutrients. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees.
